# NLP Baseline — Thesis-Ready Methods and Results

*Drop-in prose for the thesis NLP chapter. Every number below is reproduced directly from `NLP_Baseline_Results_v1.0.xlsx`, generated by `15_Scripts/alcsm_nlp_baseline_v1.0.py` (fixed seed 42) — see `NLP_Baseline_Report_v1.0.md` for the full technical account this prose summarizes.*

---

## Methods

To assess whether an automated system can approximate the human-coded ALCSM scores, a minimal, interpretable baseline was implemented rather than a more elaborate architecture, consistent with the scope of an MSc thesis. The baseline was trained entirely on infrastructure available locally, without recourse to any external API or hosted language model, on the same underlying LinkedIn-derived profile fields available to the human annotators — never on the annotation process's own evidence text or scoring rationale, which would have leaked each label's justification directly into the model's input.

For each profile, a single text document was constructed by concatenating five categories of structured profile information: current role details (title, industry, company size, seniority category), education history (degree level, field of study, institution), certifications (category, name, issuing organization), professional experience (job titles, industry, a coarse tenure bucket, and binary leadership/AI-relatedness flags per role), and technical contributions (type and title). Employer names and geographic fields were deliberately excluded, as they carry no scoring-relevant signal for any ALCSM dimension and needlessly increase re-identification risk.

Each of the six ALCSM dimensions (D1–D6) was modeled independently, consistent with ALCSM's status as a formative index whose dimensions are not expected to be interchangeable or combinable. No composite or pooled score was computed at any stage. For each dimension, profile documents were transformed into a term-frequency–inverse-document-frequency (TF-IDF) representation (unigrams and bigrams, vocabulary capped at 2,000 terms, minimum document frequency of 2), and a ridge regression model was fit to predict the 0–5 ordinal score. Because the target is ordinal rather than nominal, predictions were rounded to the nearest integer and clipped to the valid [0, 5] range — a simple, standard way to respect ordinal structure without requiring a specialized ordinal-classification library.

Data were split 80/20 into training and test sets separately for each dimension, using a fixed random seed (42) for full reproducibility. Splits were stratified by score wherever every score category contained at least two profiles; where a category was too sparse to stratify (D3, whose present-only population contains exactly one profile scored 0), a plain random split was used instead and this deviation is recorded explicitly rather than silently applied. No profile appeared in both the training and test set for any dimension. All feature extraction (vectorizer vocabulary) and model fitting were performed on the training partition only, with the test partition held out and never used to influence preprocessing, vocabulary selection, or model parameters.

Profiles for which a given dimension was recorded as `unavailable` in the frozen annotation (i.e., no observable evidence existed for that dimension) were excluded from that dimension's training and evaluation entirely, never treated as an observed score of zero.

Model performance was evaluated per dimension using exact-match rate, mean absolute error, and linear-weighted Cohen's kappa (appropriate for an ordinal 0–5 scale, penalizing larger disagreements more than adjacent ones), together with the full confusion matrix. Each dimension's result was additionally compared against a majority-class baseline (always predicting that dimension's most common training-set score), to distinguish genuine predictive signal from the trivial floor set by class imbalance — a comparison of particular importance for D5, whose training population is dominated (87%) by a single score.

## Results

Table 1 summarizes per-dimension performance for the six independently trained models, evaluated against the frozen human gold standard.

**Table 1. TF-IDF + ridge regression baseline performance, by ALCSM dimension.**

| Dimension | n (test) | Exact match | MAE | Weighted κ | Majority-class baseline | Exceeds baseline? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| D1 — Formal Education | 95 | 0.295 | 0.989 | 0.283 | 0.284 | Marginally |
| D2 — Professional Certifications | 47 | 1.000 | 0.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | No (degenerate target, see below) |
| D3 — Practical AI Experience | 100 | 0.520 | 0.570 | 0.399 | 0.350 | Yes |
| D4 — Technical Contributions | 35 | 0.629 | 0.371 | −0.022 | 0.714 | No |
| D5 — Leadership & Strategic Responsibility | 100 | 0.870 | 0.150 | 0.260 | 0.870 | No (tie) |
| D6 — AI Industry/Application Breadth | 100 | 0.440 | 0.640 | 0.238 | 0.480 | No |

Model performance was markedly uneven across dimensions, and this unevenness is itself a substantive finding rather than a shortcoming of the evaluation. D2 achieved perfect exact-match agreement, but this figure is not evidence of model competence: once profiles with no certification evidence are correctly excluded, the remaining population is uniformly scored 1 by the human annotator, leaving nothing to discriminate — any constant predictor, including the majority-class baseline, achieves the same result. This mirrors an independent finding from the inter-rater reliability analysis (`RQ3_Reliability_Final_Interpretation_v1.0.md`), where D2 similarly showed perfect but degenerate agreement between two human raters for the same underlying reason.

D5 showed a comparable pattern: the model matched, but did not exceed, its 87% majority-class floor, reflecting the severe class imbalance already documented in the human annotation (87% of profiles scored exactly 3). Its modestly positive weighted kappa (0.260) indicates the model did capture some real signal beyond the constant baseline — inspection of the model's most positively and negatively weighted terms shows "head," "director," and "transformation officer" associated with higher predicted scores and "lead" and "ai lead" with lower ones, mirroring a distinction the human reliability analysis independently identified as a genuine point of rater disagreement — but this signal is too weak to be visible in the exact-match rate alone, illustrating why exact-match accuracy is an insufficient metric for an imbalanced ordinal target.

D4 and D6 did not exceed their majority-class baselines. For D4, this likely reflects the small usable training set (140 profiles, since technical-contribution evidence is present for only 175 of 500 profiles). For D6, inspection of the confusion matrix shows the model's predictions cluster almost entirely at scores 1–2, rarely reaching the higher scores (3–5) that do occur in the real population; a plausible explanation is that D6 requires counting the number of *distinct* industries or application domains represented across a profile's full experience history — a signal that a bag-of-words text representation, which does not explicitly aggregate or count across repeated structured fields, is poorly positioned to capture.

D1 and D3 showed the clearest evidence of genuine, if modest, learned signal. D3's result is notable in contrast to the reliability findings: it was the dimension with the weakest human inter-rater reliability (α = 0.10) in the parallel double-coding analysis, yet the baseline model exceeded its majority-class floor by the widest margin of any dimension (52.0% vs. 35.0% exact match). This is reported as an interesting asymmetry rather than a resolution of D3's reliability problem — a model trained against one rater's scores can find consistent surface-level lexical correlates (terms such as "ai," "data scientist," and tenure-length indicators) even where two independent human raters genuinely disagreed on how those same cues should be weighted at the score-boundary level.

## Interpretation

Taken together, these results support a qualified answer to the stated objective: a minimal, local, fully reproducible NLP baseline can approximate some ALCSM dimensions — most clearly D1 and D3 — better than trivial guessing, while for others (D2, D4, D5, D6) it either cannot meaningfully be distinguished from a majority-class baseline or is outperformed by one, for reasons traceable to specific, identifiable properties of each dimension (degenerate class distribution, small sample size, or a signal structure not well suited to a bag-of-words representation). No dimension's result is used, or should be read, as evidence for or against ALCSM's underlying validity as a measurement framework — that is a separate question, addressed through the reliability and content-validity evidence reported elsewhere (`07_Reliability/`). This baseline instead demonstrates what a defensible, minimal automation attempt looks like against this gold standard, and where its current limits lie, which is exactly the evidence RQ5 requires at this stage.
